newsitem.title: USA: Dole's voice gets weaker in last campaign day struggle.
newsitem.headline: Dole's voice gets weaker in last campaign day struggle.

text.p: Fighting fatique, losing his voice and running out of time, Bob Dole struggled on Monday to mount a last-ditch drive to pull off an upset victory over President Bill Clinton on Tuesday.
At a late night rally here, the Republican candidate battled through his speech in a hoarse whisper, saying he had to tell running mate Jack Kemp to give most of his speech when he preceeded him.
"I've given about 23 speechs ... in the last 24 hours," Dole said.

In rally after rally, Dole urged people to vote as he rushed through California by bus and plane for the state's 54 electoral votes -- the richest election prize in the nation with nearly one out of every five of the 270 electoral votes needed to win.

"We're gonna win on Nov. 5," said Dole in West Covina Sunday night "because I trust the people and President Clinton trusts the government and my word is good" then losing his sandpaper-rough voice temporarily.
"I will tell the truth, as long as my voice holds out I'll tell the truth," he quickly added.

"You can make a difference ... 54 big ones," Dole growled about the electoral number in Loma Linda at a sunset picnic with Kemp in a field surrounded by orange groves and some 4,000 party stalwarts. Democratic hecklers shouted in the background well away from the partisan crowd.
He said he was aiming for a historic upset like the 1948 stunner when Democrat Harry Truman beat Tom Dewey.
Dole held up a copy of the 1948 Chicago Tribune with the bold headline "Dewey defeats Truman," and told the crowd "I never met President Dewey."
"They used to say 'Harry give 'em hell' and he said 'I'm going to tell them the truth and they'll think it's hell -- and that's what we're gonna do in the next 48 hours," he said.

Dole planned to campaign Truman-style and close out his campaign before in Truman's hometown of Independence, Missouri, on Tuesday after a breakneck charge through Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Louisiana, Tennesee and Iowa.

Last stop: his prairie crossroads hometown of Russell, Kansas, to vote on Tuesday with his wife, Elizabeth, who has been travelling with him on his much-promoted last 96 hours of campaigning almost non-stop since last Friday morning starting in Columbus, Ohio.
"I haven't stayed up around the clock since I fought the Nazis in World War II," said Dole, whose right arm remains useless from combat wounds that nearly killed him.
The 73-year-old campaigner was behind in polls that also showed wide disinterest in this election.

But he took comfort from some polls showing the gap closing as he hammered away at Clinton's ethics amid a number of investigations with the latest being questionable contributions to Clinton's Democratic Party from people with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.

For about three weeks Dole has shifted from his earlier economic programme theme -- a 15 percent tax rate cut plan that has never fully caught the public fancy -- to an attack on ethical lapses in the White House.
"I believe the election will determine -- does character count. And if the American people say it doesn't, I will be surprised," Dole said in Loma Linda.
Reciting Clinton promises and programmes, Dole asked "do you trust this man?"

Grabbing for every vote, Dole appealed to supporters of Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to vote Republican. "I don't want to get into a quarrel about Ross Perot but when you vote for Ross Perot you vote for Bill Clinton," said Dole.
He said there are many states that are close and the Perot vote "can make a difference."

"And Perot doesn't want Bill Clinton, and I know that for certain, so if you are a Perot supporter and you want to defeat Bill Clinton what do you do -- you vote for Bob Dole and Jack Kemp," said Dole.
Dole surrounded himself with politicians, such as California Gov. Pete Wilson, and celebrities like movie actress Bo Derek and singer Marie Osmond.
